title: Education and Health: Evaluating Theories and Evidence
research_question: How does educational attainment affect health outcomes and health-related behaviors, and through what mechanisms—such as income, occupation, access to care, information and cognitive skills, preferences, social rank, or networks—does education translate into better health? To what extent is the observed education-health gradient causal, and what are its implications for the monetary value of education and for public policy?
data_description: The analysis primarily uses the U.S. National Health Interview Survey (NHIS) waves from 1990, 1991, and 2000, including the Health Promotion and Disease Prevention Supplement (1990), the Drug and Alcohol Use Supplement (1991), and the Person and Adult Sample (2000). The sample is restricted to individuals aged 25 and older. Outcomes include 5-year mortality (constructed by linking 1990 NHIS to the National Death Index through 1996), self-reports of acute and chronic disease diagnoses (heart disease, cancer, stroke, diabetes, hypertension, etc.), self-rated health, anxiety and depression scales, functional limitations, and a wide range of health behaviors (smoking, drinking, BMI/obesity, exercise, illegal drug use, seat belt use, smoke detectors, preventive screenings, vaccinations, and disease management). Covariates include age, race, gender, Hispanic ethnicity, family income, family size, region, MSA, marital status, insurance, occupation, and industry. Cross-country life expectancy is examined using Barro-Lee education data.
institutional_context: The setting is the persistent socioeconomic gradient in health observed across developed countries, where more-educated individuals live longer, suffer fewer chronic and acute diseases, report better mental and physical functioning, and engage in healthier behaviors. In the United States, age-adjusted mortality among high-school dropouts aged 25–64 in 1999 was more than twice that of those with some college, and these disparities have been widening since the 1980s alongside rising labor-market returns to schooling. Health inequalities by education are explicit policy targets in the U.S. Healthy People 2010 initiative and in U.K. health policy. The paper situates its inquiry against historical changes in compulsory schooling laws, expansions of college access, public-health information shocks (e.g., the 1964 Surgeon General Report on smoking), and the diffusion of medical innovations, all of which differentially affect education groups and motivate questions about whether education subsidies should be viewed as health policy.
